summary: This informational note identifies key Internet Protocol Suite protocols for use in the Smart Grid. It helps people building a Smart Grid profile choose what to select from the suite.

plainLanguage.summary: The electric grid is becoming a smart network. This lists which internet tools fit that job, like a shopping list.

questions: which ip protocols for smart grid
ipv4 or ipv6 for smart grid
subtitle: Which Internet Protocol Suite protocols are essential for building and operating a smart electrical grid.

tldr.problem: The Smart Grid—a modernized electrical system with digital communications—requires a complex mix of Internet and application protocols. Engineers designing Smart Grid networks need guidance on which protocols from the vast Internet Protocol Suite are relevant and how to profile them for their use cases.
tldr.mechanism: This document surveys the Internet Protocol Suite layers (Application, Transport, Network, Media) and identifies specific protocols that are critical for Smart Grid deployment: security protocols, routing protocols, management protocols, service discovery, and application-layer protocols. It explains the role of each layer and the security considerations at each level.
tldr.outcome: Smart Grid architects can reference this document as a roadmap for selecting appropriate Internet protocols, understanding how they interact, and implementing security at each layer.

today: RFC 6272 is an Informational RFC providing guidance for Smart Grid protocol selection. It has not been obsoleted. As the Smart Grid continues to evolve, IPv6 adoption is accelerating and new protocols for resource-constrained devices are gaining traction. The document remains relevant as a reference for understanding which IETF protocols apply to Smart Grid deployments.

sections.title: Smart Grids and Internet Protocols
sections.content:
A Smart Grid is a modernized electrical network that uses digital communications to monitor and control power generation, transmission, distribution, and consumption. It allows two-way communication between utilities and customers, enabling responsive demand management, integration of renewable energy sources, and real-time monitoring of grid conditions.

Data communications technologies are used throughout the Smart Grid: to monitor power flows, maintain equipment, manage operations, and coordinate with customers. The Smart Grid is fundamentally a collection of interconnected computer networks serving electrical utilities and their customers. This document helps Smart Grid architects profile the Internet Protocol Suite (IPS) for their needs—deciding which protocols to implement, how they interact, and what security measures each layer requires.
sections.plainLanguage: The electric grid is becoming smart by adding computers and networks. This document helps builders pick the right internet tools for the job.

sections.title: Layers of the Internet Protocol Suite
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol Suite organizes communication into four layers: Application, Transport, Network, and Media Layers (Data Link and Physical). Unlike the ISO-OSI model, the Internet model compresses the presentation and session layers into the application layer.

The Application Layer includes protocols like SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) that do encoding, session management, and specific services. The Transport Layer is the lowest layer that travels end-to-end unmodified; it includes TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) for reliable ordered streams, UDP (User Datagram Protocol) for datagrams, SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol), and DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol). The Network Layer features IPv4 and IPv6, which identify destinations and route datagrams. The Media Layers handle physical transmission over technologies like Ethernet, optical fiber, or wireless.

Each layer is responsible for its own security. Physical and Data Link layer security addresses physical attacks and eavesdropping. Network, Transport, and Application layer security focuses on the CIA triad: Confidentiality (encryption), Integrity (authentication and data integrity checks), and Availability (resisting denial-of-service).
sections.plainLanguage: Internet communication is like a mail system: the application is what you send, transport is the mail truck, network is the postal routes, and media is the roads and vehicles carrying the trucks.

sections.title: Security Toolbox and Infrastructure Protocols
sections.content:
The IETF has developed security building blocks that protocols often reuse. Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) using RADIUS or Diameter verifies that users and devices are who they claim to be and allows access only to authorized resources. Network Layer Security via IPsec encrypts and authenticates IP traffic. Transport Layer Security (TLS) provides encrypted channels above TCP. Application Layer Security addresses security at the protocol level. Secure Shell (SSH) provides secure remote access. Public Key Infrastructure (PKIX) manages certificates for authentication, and Kerberos provides mutual authentication.

Infrastructure protocols are equally essential. The Domain Name System (DNS) translates names to IP addresses and can be secured with DNSSEC. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) assigns IP addresses and configuration to devices. Network Time Protocol (NTP) synchronizes clocks across the grid—critical for correlating events and managing power flow. Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) monitors and reports on network devices. NETCONF configures devices using XML encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Security tools prevent intruders, verify identities, encrypt messages, and manage keys. Infrastructure tools give devices addresses, synchronize clocks, and let operators check the network.

sections.title: Routing, Transport, and Application Protocols
sections.content:
Routing Protocols decide how data packets move through the grid. The Internet Protocol Suite offers several: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) is simple but limited to small networks. OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) and IS-IS calculate efficient paths based on network topology. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) connects separate autonomous systems and is essential for inter-utility communications. DYMO (Dynamic MANET On-Demand Routing) and OLSR (Optimized Link State Routing Protocol) suit wireless mobile networks. RPL (Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks) is designed for resource-constrained devices like smart meters.

Transport Layer Protocols provide end-to-end delivery. TCP guarantees reliable, ordered delivery and is suitable for important control messages. UDP is lightweight and suitable for time-sensitive telemetry. SCTP combines reliability with multi-streaming. DCCP prioritizes timely delivery over perfect reliability.

At the Application Layer, DNS (with DNSSEC) enables name-based device discovery. SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) manages voice and video sessions. XMPP (Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol) enables real-time messaging and device status updates. iCalendar coordinates time-scheduled operations like demand response events.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing protocols are the road maps. Transport protocols are the trucks (reliable big ones or fast light ones). Applications are what you send: messages, voice, or status updates.

sections.title: IPv4, IPv6, and Coexistence
sections.content:
IPv4 has been the standard for decades and is deeply embedded in Smart Grid deployments. It offers unicast routing, multicast for group communications (useful for broadcasting demand response signals), and a mature ecosystem of tools. IPv6 provides vastly more addresses (needed as the grid scales to billions of devices) and includes built-in security (IPsec in the base specification) and efficient multicast and neighbor discovery.

However, the transition from IPv4 to IPv6 is gradual. Smart Grid networks must handle Dual Stack coexistence (running both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously), Tunneling mechanisms (encapsulating IPv6 in IPv4 or vice versa), and Translation between IPv4 and IPv6 networks. Each approach has trade-offs: dual stack requires more resources, tunneling adds overhead, and translation is complex but transparent.

For address allocation, IPv4 uses DHCP or static assignment, while IPv6 can use DHCPv6 or stateless address autoconfiguration (which assigns addresses based on the network prefix without requiring a DHCP server).
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 is the old standard that everything uses now. IPv6 is the new one with way more addresses. Most networks must run both at the same time, like being bilingual.
